title: Yom Kippur: releasing vows
hook: the evening begins by annulling rash vows, sung three times

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah's rule: wrongs between people need the people first. Your line was ask before the day. Today, the first words of Yom Kippur itself.

The sun is still up. The synagogue is full, many dressed in white. The ark opens, and Torah scrolls are carried out and held on either side of the prayer leader, like witnesses. The room goes quiet. Then the cantor begins a melody so famous that composers have written concert pieces on it. The words aren't a prayer at all. They're a legal formula, in Aramaic, sung three times, each a little louder.
screen: `THE SUN IS STILL UP.` → `SCROLLS HELD LIKE WITNESSES.` → `A LEGAL FORMULA, SUNG.`

segments.voice: Kol Nidre means all vows. The text declares that all vows, oaths and promises we make to God, and fail to keep, are released, void, not binding. Why open Yom Kippur with that? The Torah takes vows seriously: "When a man voweth a vow unto the LORD, or sweareth an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word." People make rash promises to God in a moment of fear or anger: if I get through this, I'll never, I'll always. Then they can't keep them. Kol Nidre clears those words before standing in judgment. Before it begins, a line gives permission to pray together with sinners, with everyone, whatever their past. Right after comes a verse from Numbers: the whole community shall be forgiven, "and the stranger that sojourneth among them." Some important limits. Kol Nidre covers only personal vows between a person and God. It has never released promises made to other people, contracts or oaths in court. Medieval rabbis argued about it, and some great authorities wanted it removed. In later centuries, enemies of the Jews twisted it into a false charge that a Jew's word couldn't be trusted, which it never meant. Rabbeinu Tam championed a change in the wording, to look forward: vows from this Yom Kippur to the next. Many Ashkenazi communities say it that way. Its staying power may be the melody, and the honesty. Who in that room has never said something to heaven and then not kept it?
screen: `KOL NIDRE: ALL VOWS.` · `RASH PROMISES TO GOD.` · `NEVER PROMISES TO PEOPLE.` · `FROM THIS YOM KIPPUR TO THE NEXT.` · then, large: `RELEASE THE VOWS.`

segments.voice: Think of something you vowed to yourself, or to heaven, in a hard moment, that you haven't kept and maybe never could, like I'll never eat sugar again or I'll call every day, and name it honestly. Then set it down with relief, not guilt: if you pray, bring it to God and ask to be released; if not, simply say, I set this down. Then ask whether a smaller, real promise belongs in its place.
Kol Nidre. All vows. The Aramaic formula, sung three times at the start of Yom Kippur, releasing unkept personal vows to God.
Your line: release the vows. The promises you made to other people still stand. Day six hundred fifty-three.
